description:
Robotics Portfolio for MSc & PhD Applications (2027)

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

A strong robotics portfolio is three to five projects that prove you can build, simulate or control a real robotic system end-to-end — each with code, a short video and an honest write-up of what failed. Supervisors shortlist on evidence of working systems, not on enthusiasm or course lists.

What supervisors actually look at

Robotics faculty reviewing MSc or PhD applications spend minutes per candidate. In that window they check, roughly in order:

  1. Does anything you've built actually work? A video of a quadruped recovering from a push, a manipulator inserting a connector, a locomotion policy surviving unseen terrain — ten seconds of working evidence beats a page of coursework descriptions.
  2. Can you code? They will open the GitHub link. Clean repos with READMEs pass; empty or copy-pasted repos sink applications.
  3. Do you understand what you did? The write-up matters less for polish than for evidence of judgement: what you tried, what failed, what you'd do differently.

This is why a portfolio is your most controllable application asset — unlike grades, you can build it deliberately over 6–12 months. Pair it with a tight CV that references each project in one line.

The portfolio that works: 3–5 projects

Project typeWhat it provesEffort level
Simulation RL project (e.g. locomotion policy in Isaac Gym/MuJoCo, with a metrics table)You can train, evaluate and honestly report learned controllers4–8 weeks
Classical control project (e.g. whole-body or joint-space controller on a sim humanoid/arm, with tracking-error plots)You know the model-based foundations the field still runs on4–8 weeks
Hardware project (even small: a balance robot, a gripper with force feedback)You can debug real systems — the scarcest skillVariable, highest impact
Reproduction of a published paper (with deviations documented)You read literature critically and can implement it2–4 weeks
Competition entry (e.g. simulation challenges, robotics competitions)Teamwork under constraints; externally judged resultsSeasonal

Ideal balance for a humanoid robotics applicant: one learning-based project, one model-based project, one hardware or competition item, one rigorous paper reproduction. That spread answers the question every panel asks — can this person do both worlds? Our humanoid robotics research topics list gives directions sized for exactly these projects.

Presenting each project: the five-element format

Give every project the same five elements. Consistency signals professionalism:

  1. One-sentence claim. "Trained a quadruped locomotion policy that walks on five unseen terrain types at 0.8 m/s."
  2. Video. 30–60 seconds, no music, showing the system working (and, briefly, failing — honesty reads well).
  3. Repository. Public, with a README covering setup, structure and how to reproduce the main result.
  4. Results table or plot. Numbers against a baseline, however simple. "Better than a hand-tuned PD controller by X%" is a real result.
  5. Honest limitations paragraph. 3–5 sentences on what doesn't work. This is the single most trust-building element — and the one most applicants skip.

Common mistakes that sink otherwise good candidates

  • Course-project dumps. Six repos of unmodified coursework with no READMEs. Curate: three strong items beat ten unexplained ones.
  • Missing media. A robotics project without a video forces the reviewer to imagine it working. They won't.
  • Notebook-only ML work. A Colab notebook fine-tuning an existing model is not a robotics project unless it closes a perception-action loop.
  • Overclaiming. "Built a humanoid AI" for a simulated walking controller destroys credibility with exactly the readers who matter. Describe scale honestly.
  • Dead links. Check every link the week you submit — including the one in your CV, cover letter and supervisor emails.

A 6-month build plan

If you're starting from coursework only:

MonthGoal
1–2Paper reproduction or structured course (e.g. a legged-robotics or RL specialisation) with all assignments made public and written up
3–4One substantial simulation project with baselines, metrics and video
5One hardware or competition item, however small — a balancing robot counts
6Polish: READMEs, videos, a one-page portfolio site or pinned GitHub profile, links inserted into CV and applications

Then connect it to applications: reference specific projects in your humanoid robotics PhD proposal and in every supervisor email — "project X is why I believe I can contribute to your Y project" converts a portfolio from decoration into argument.

Frequently asked questions

How many projects do I need for a robotics PhD application? Three to five well-presented projects are plenty. Quality and honesty of presentation matter far more than count — one excellent, documented project outperforms six unexplained repos.

Is simulation-only experience enough if I have no hardware access? Yes, especially for humanoid and legged robotics, where much research is simulation-first. Add a small hardware item if you ever can (a cheap balancing or manipulator kit), but a rigorous simulation portfolio with real baselines is a legitimate path.

Should I put my portfolio on a personal website or just GitHub? GitHub is where reviewers look; a simple one-page site linking the best three projects with videos helps non-roboticist committee members. Do both, keep them in sync, and make sure every link works before submitting.

Do MSc applications need a portfolio too? A lighter version helps at selective programmes: one or two projects with code and video strengthens an application that grades alone can't. The same presentation format applies, just with fewer items.

Official source

Application requirements differ by programme — some ask for portfolios explicitly, others only via the CV. Check each university's official admissions page for what may be submitted and how (links vs. attachments), and verify deadlines there.
